evidence.snippet: Persons with asthma and multiple diagnoses reported odorous/pungent and building-related environmental factors to trigger symptoms to a larger extent than did the reference group, mainly due to perfume and odors from flowers.
evidence.explanation: This supports the role of environmental factors in triggering symptoms in people with asthma but does not specifically address allergens as a triggering factor.

evidence.snippet: The link between asthma and food allergy has been well researched over the years; although the exact interplay between the two atopic conditions is yet to be fully described. Research suggests that children who have both asthma and food allergy are at greater risk of more severe asthmatic episodes.
evidence.explanation: This supports the idea that allergens (specifically food allergies) can trigger severe asthma attacks.

evidence.snippet: A complex interplay of genetic predisposition and environmental influences results in the clinical picture of allergic asthma.
evidence.explanation: This supports the role of environmental influences, which includes allergens, in allergic asthma.

evidence.snippet: The implementation of policies to reduce environmental allergic triggers can be an important adjunct to optimal patient care for allergic rhinitis and allergic asthma.
evidence.explanation: It supports that allergic asthma can be triggered by environmental allergens.

evidence.snippet: The rising frequency of obstructive respiratory diseases during recent years, in particular allergic asthma, can be partially explained by changes in the environment, with the increasing presence in the atmosphere of chemical triggers (particulate matter and gaseous components such as nitrogen dioxide and ozone) and biologic triggers (aeroallergens).
evidence.explanation: This directly supports the role of environmental allergens as triggers for allergic asthma.

evidence.snippet: For patients with asthma, exacerbations and poor control can result from exposure to environmental triggers, such as allergens and air particulates.
evidence.explanation: This supports the idea of allergens being environmental triggers for asthma.

evidence.snippet: Environmental exposures varied across the year and demonstrated seasonal patterns.
evidence.explanation: This supports the role of environmental allergens like mold in triggering asthma.

evidence.snippet: SIRT1, an NAD+-dependent deacetylase, exerting protective effects by inhibiting NF-κB and STAT3, activating Nrf2 and FOXO3, and suppressing TGF-β/Smad.
evidence.explanation: This review identifies the key molecular mechanisms through which SIRT1 exerts protective effects in asthma by targeting multiple pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic pathways.

evidence.snippet: In asthma, SIRT1 attenuates Th2 inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and airway smooth muscle proliferation
evidence.explanation: This review explicitly describes SIRT1's protective effects specific to asthma pathophysiology, directly addressing three key pathological mechanisms.

evidence.snippet: Shared benefits include mitigation of oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and extracellular matrix remodeling.
evidence.explanation: Describes SIRT1's shared protective mechanisms across multiple pathophysiological domains relevant to asthma and COPD.

steps/10.description: SIRT1 (Sirtuin 1), an NAD+-dependent deacetylase, exerts protective effects in asthma by inhibiting pro-inflammatory signaling pathways (NF-κB, STAT3) while activating stress-response transcription factors (Nrf2, FOXO3) and suppressing pro-fibrotic TGF-β/Smad signaling. SIRT1 activation attenuates Th2 inflammation, suppresses mucus hypersecretion and goblet cell metaplasia, and reduces airway smooth muscle proliferation. SIRT1 also mitigates oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: In asthma, it includes alterations of the epithelial cell layer with goblet cell hyperplasia, thickening of basement membranes, peri-bronchial and peri-bronchoalveolar fibrosis.
evidence.explanation: The reference acknowledges that airway remodeling in asthma involves changes to the epithelial cell layer, fibroblasts, and smooth muscle cells.

evidence.snippet: In the long-term, asthma may become moderately to fully irreversible. Severe, irreversible airflow obstruction may develop despite apparently appropriate therapy.
evidence.explanation: The reference supports the idea that long-standing inflammation can result in irreversible structural changes affecting lung function.

evidence.snippet: Structural changes reported in the airways of asthmatics include epithelial fragility, goblet cell hyperplasia, enlarged submucosal mucus glands, angiogenesis, increased matrix deposition in the airway wall, increased airway smooth muscle mass, wall thickening and abnormalities in elastin.
evidence.explanation: The reference details structural changes involving various cell types, including epithelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and other airway structures resulting from long-term inflammation in asthma.

evidence.snippet: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways interacting with altered structure and function of the formed elements including smooth muscle.
evidence.explanation: The reference confirms that chronic inflammation in asthma involves structural alterations involving smooth muscle cells and other components, supporting airway remodeling.

evidence.snippet: Two airway cell types are critical for asthma pathogenesis: epithelial cells and smooth muscle cells.
evidence.explanation: The reference highlights the importance of epithelial cells and smooth muscle cells in asthma pathogenesis, supporting the role of these cell types in airway remodeling.

steps/12.description: Viral lower respiratory wheezing illnesses in infancy and early childhood, particularly those caused by human rhinovirus (and to a lesser extent respiratory syncytial virus), are among the strongest early-life predictors of subsequent childhood asthma. In a high-risk prospective birth cohort, wheezing with rhinovirus in the first three years of life conferred an almost ten-fold increase in the odds of asthma at age 6, an effect that grew stronger when wheezing occurred later in early childhood. Rhinovirus infection of the developing airway epithelium interacts with allergic (type 2) sensitization to injure and remodel the epithelium and bias the immune response toward the Th2 program, contributing to asthma inception rather than acting purely as a marker of pre-existing susceptibility. This positions early respiratory infection as an upstream, potentially modifiable contributor to the chronic airway inflammation that defines established asthma.

steps/13.description: Allergic asthma is driven by a type 2 immune response in which allergen-activated dendritic cells promote Th2 cell differentiation. Th2 cells and ILC2s produce IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, which drive IgE class switching, eosinophil recruitment and survival, goblet cell metaplasia, and airway hyperresponsiveness. IL-4/IL-13 signal through STAT6 to amplify the type 2 program, while IL-5 is the principal regulator of eosinophil maturation and survival, acting through the IL-5 receptor alpha subunit carried by eosinophils; IL-4, IL-13 and epithelial alarmins modulate tissue recruitment and amplification of the inflammation.

steps/15.description: Group 1 house dust mite (HDM) allergens, exemplified by the cysteine peptidase Der p 1, are potent triggers of intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in airway epithelial cells, an event relevant to asthma because the disease is associated with deficits in antioxidant defences and because ROS amplify inflammation through transcription-factor and chromatin regulation. Der p 1 behaves as a prothrombinase, generating thrombin that activates protease-activated receptors (PAR1/PAR4); the resulting signaling, converging with purinoceptor (P2X7/P2Y) activation by ATP released through pannexons, drives sheddase activity of the metalloprotease ADAM10. ADAM10 in turn sustains further prothrombin activation, establishing a self-amplifying thrombin-ROS signaling cycle. As the principal sheddase of the adherens-junction protein E-cadherin, ADAM10 activation also compounds the epithelial-barrier disruption caused by direct cleavage of tight junctions by group 1 HDM allergens, and ADAM10 liberates chemokines (CCL20, CCL2, CCL5, CXCL8) and promotes TH2 bias and IgE synthesis (via CD23 shedding) - tying allergen-protease sensing to the type 2 inflammatory program of allergic asthma.

evidence.snippet: The predominant mechanism for PGS×C is the amplification of genetic effects in adverse contexts, such as low polyunsaturated fatty acids or social determinants of ill health
evidence.explanation: Direct source (Nagpal & Gibson 2026): across seven UK Biobank diseases and 75 contexts, amplification of genetic effects in adverse contexts is identified as the predominant mechanism of PGS×context interaction — the mechanism applied in this hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: GxSex is pervasive but acts primarily through systematic sex differences in the magnitude of many genetic effects
evidence.explanation: Corroborates amplification — systematic differences in the magnitude of polygenic effects rather than in the identity of causal variants — as the primary mode of gene-by-context interaction.

hypotheses/0.description: Polygenic-score-by-context (PGS×C) interactions reported for asthma in the UK Biobank appear to reflect amplification rather than context-specific causal variants: the same susceptibility loci (e.g. IL4, IL13, HLA-DQ, CDHR3) exert systematically larger effects in disease-promoting contexts. This entry proposes that the amplification arises because polygenic liability and adverse exposures — tobacco smoke, air pollution and allergen load — converge on the shared Airway Inflammation node, so their joint effect on the liability-threshold scale is super-additive rather than additive. Nagpal & Gibson (Nat Genet 2026, PMID:42443528) include asthma among the seven diseases showing pervasive PGS×context interactions in the UK Biobank.

open_questions/0.rationale: Population PGS×context analyses (Nagpal & Gibson 2026, PMID:42443528) are largely unable to establish the causality of specific contexts. For asthma the biochemical "contexts" (blood eosinophils, total IgE) are readouts of type 2 airway inflammation and atopy rather than upstream drivers, and behavioural exposures such as activity or occupational avoidance may change in response to symptomatic disease. Distinguishing genuine amplification of genetic effects from reverse causation determines whether the modelled exposure reductions (smoke, pollution, allergen avoidance) would actually reduce risk.

open_questions/1.rationale: The asthma entry captures type 2 signaling, mucus overproduction, and airway remodeling, but it does not yet distinguish reversible inflammatory epithelial states from remodeled mucous-cell states that continue after the trigger is removed. Recent human airway-epithelium perturbation data make this a tractable causal experiment rather than a descriptive subtype problem.

evidence.snippet: In asthma, SIRT1 attenuates Th2 inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and airway smooth muscle proliferation
evidence.explanation: Establishes the candidate SIRT1-protective phenotypes (Th2 inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, smooth muscle proliferation) whose cell-type causal dependence the proposed experiment aims to dissect.

evidence.snippet: clinical translation faces critical barriers: cell type-specific SIRT1 effects, pharmacokinetic limitations of current activators, and lack of biomarker-guided strategies.
evidence.explanation: Directly states the unresolved translational barriers (cell-type-specific effects, pharmacokinetic limits of activators, and missing biomarker-guided selection) that motivate this knowledge gap.

open_questions/2.rationale: SIRT1 is reported to protect against asthmatic airway disease by inhibiting NF-kB and STAT3, activating Nrf2 and FOXO3, and suppressing TGF-beta/Smad, thereby attenuating Th2 inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and airway smooth muscle proliferation. However, SIRT1's net effect is cell-type specific: deacetylation of distinct substrates in CD4+ T cells, airway epithelial/goblet cells, and airway smooth muscle cells may engage opposing programs, so a benefit measured in one compartment cannot be assumed to hold across the airway. The asthma entry captures type 2 signaling, mucus overproduction, and airway remodeling as separate nodes but does not yet resolve which of these is causally dependent on SIRT1 activity in which cell type. Translation is further limited by pharmacokinetic barriers of current SIRT1 activators and by the absence of biomarker-guided strategies to select responders. What remains unresolved is whether cell-type-targeted restoration of SIRT1 activity reduces type 2 inflammation and mucous metaplasia without provoking off-target effects, and which measurable biomarker predicts that response. Resolving this would convert SIRT1 from a broadly cytoprotective pathway into a stratified, compartment-specific therapeutic target.

evidence.snippet: Despite substantial technical challenges and unresolved questions regarding generalizability and heterogeneity, such investigative strategies are expected to enhance our understanding of asthma endotypes and the development of more effective, precision-based preventive and therapeutic interventions.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly identifies heterogeneity in G×E interaction mechanisms across asthma endotypes as mechanistically unresolved and a priority for precision medicine approaches.

evidence.snippet: Investigating gene-environment (G × E) interactions holds significant potential to elucidate the regulatory genetic architecture underlying individual responses to environmental risk factors in childhood asthma.
evidence.explanation: Identifies G×E investigation as essential for understanding how genetic variants modulate individual responses to environmental exposures and drive endotype-specific disease patterns.

open_questions/3.rationale: Asthma exhibits multiple phenotypic endotypes (eosinophilic, neutrophilic, exercise-induced, occupational), and the entry documents some key mechanisms (Th2 signaling, early-life viral infection). However, the molecular bases for how genetic variants interact with distinct environmental exposures (prenatal vs. postnatal, allergen vs. pollutant vs. infection vs. occupational agent) to produce specific endotypes remain mechanistically unresolved. This gap is mechanistically important because genetic risk alleles do not always produce the same phenotype across environmental contexts, and precision interventions may require endotype-specific, G×E-informed targeting. A comprehensive mechanism linking G×E combinations to endotype selection would move beyond phenomenological endotype classification toward causal models.

steps/5.description: BLM normally cooperates with TOP3A, RMI1, and RMI2 in the BTRR complex to dissolve double Holliday junctions without crossover. Loss of BLM removes this anti-crossover genome-maintenance activity.

evidence.snippet: The absence of a functional BLM protein causes chromosome instability, excessive homologous recombination, and a greatly increased number of sister chromatid exchanges that are pathognomonic of the syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The cellular evidence identifies excessive homologous recombination after loss of functional BLM; SCE is retained as its diagnostic readout.

steps/6.description: BLM-deficient cells undergo excessive homologous recombination and mitotic crossover. Elevated sister-chromatid exchange is modeled as a cellular readout of this state rather than as a separate causal driver.

evidence.snippet: LOH is increased by fivefold or more, implying significantly increased interhomolog crossing over.

steps/7.description: Excessive interhomolog crossover recurrently removes heterozygosity across the genome, increasing the probability that cancer-relevant somatic variants become homozygous.

evidence.snippet: Among the 290 individuals in the BSR, 155 (53%) participants developed 251 malignant neoplasms; 100 (65%) were diagnosed with 1 malignancy, whereas the remaining 55 (35%) developed multiple malignancies.
evidence.explanation: The registry study documents the broad and frequently multiple cancer burden in molecularly defined Bloom syndrome.

steps/8.description: Accumulating somatic genome alterations produce a broad, early-onset cancer predisposition affecting hematologic and solid-tumor lineages, often with multiple primary cancers in one person.

evidence.snippet: Irradiated Blm-deficient mice (Blmm3/m3) exhibited an increased risk for tumors, particularly hematological malignancies
evidence.explanation: An irradiated Blm-deficient mouse model shows radiation raising tumour risk on a BLM-deficient background, which is the mechanism this edge asserts. Model-organism evidence, so it does not by itself establish the effect in patients.

edges/26.description: Radiation-induced double-strand breaks add lesions to a genome that already mis-resolves recombination intermediates without BLM, so the exposure adds to an existing predisposition rather than initiating it. EXACERBATES rather than TRIGGERS because the biallelic BLM lesion is what establishes the cancer predisposition.

evidence.snippet: Although there are no evidence-based data linking specific chemotherapeutic agents to an increased risk of secondary malignancies, most treating clinicians recommend against the use of alkylating agents, particularly busulfan, cyclophosphamide, or melphalan, due to their direct interaction with DNA.
evidence.explanation: Records both the practice recommendation and, in the same sentence, that it rests on mechanism and clinical judgement rather than on comparative outcome data.

edges/27.description: DNA-damaging cytotoxics are given against a first cancer and add genomic lesions to cells that already mis-resolve recombination intermediates, which is the stated reason for avoiding alkylating agents in this population. Registry acute myeloid leukaemias in Bloom syndrome followed chemotherapy for a prior tumour.

evidence.snippet: The presence of chain-terminating mutations in the candidate gene in persons with BS proved that it was BLM.
evidence.explanation: The gene-discovery study established causal BLM loss-of-function variants in affected individuals.

evidence.snippet: BLM | HGNC:1058 | Bloom syndrome | MONDO:0008876 | AR | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the BLM-Bloom syndrome gene-disease relationship as definitive with autosomal recessive inheritance.

evidence.snippet: A common founder mutation designated blmAsh is present in about 1 in 100 persons of Eastern European Jewish ancestry, and there are additional recurrent founder mutations among other populations.
evidence.explanation: The review reports the ancestry-associated blmAsh founder allele while noting other population-specific founders.

genes/0.notes: Pathogenic variants on both alleles establish Bloom syndrome. The common blmAsh founder allele is enriched in people of Eastern European Jewish ancestry, but this founder effect does not narrow the global disease definition.

evidence.explanation: Adds the dermatologic component of surveillance, which is the organ-specific counterpart to the ultraviolet exposure recorded as a risk factor.

treatments/3.description: Intensive surveillance includes Wilms-tumor abdominal ultrasound in early childhood, leukemia/lymphoma symptom review, non-ionizing whole-body MRI from adolescence, early colorectal screening, and early breast MRI. The schedule should follow current predisposition guidance and specialist care.

evidence.snippet: In persons with cancer, modification of chemotherapy dosage and duration per oncologist.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends individualized oncologist-directed modification.

evidence.snippet: Alkylating agents and radiation therapy are considered high risk and are avoided when possible in those with BSyn.
evidence.explanation: The source supports minimizing particularly hazardous modalities.

evidence.snippet: We recommend starting at lower doses and escalating as tolerated, with close monitoring for toxicity as further dose modifications may be required in order to complete therapy.
evidence.explanation: Gives the dosing strategy behind individualized reduced-toxicity therapy, namely starting low, escalating to tolerance, and expecting further modification.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, significant dose reductions ranging from 20-60% of typical dosing of many of the other chemotherapeutic agents allowed for tolerable toxicities in our patients throughout treatment with remission induction in our patient with AML and long-term remission in our patient with ALL.
evidence.explanation: Two patients treated at 20 to 60 percent of standard doses tolerated therapy and entered remission, which is the outcome evidence that dose reduction need not mean undertreatment. Two cases, so the range is a reported experience rather than a validated schedule.

evidence.snippet: It is noteworthy that all patients who achieved remission had undergone dose reductions in chemotherapy, tailored to individual tolerance.
evidence.explanation: In the largest paediatric series, every remission occurred under individually tailored dose reduction, supporting individualization rather than a fixed protocol.

evidence.snippet: However, five achieved remission, highlighting the possibility of curative treatment despite significant toxicities.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that curative intent remains achievable, which is the counterweight to reflexive undertreatment.

treatments/4.description: Cancer treatment is individualized by oncology specialists, commonly with reduced dosage or duration because standard regimens can cause excessive toxicity. Ionizing radiation and alkylating agents are minimized or avoided when clinically feasible; undertreatment is also a risk, so no universal dose reduction is asserted.

evidence.snippet: Annual fasting blood glucose and hemoglobin A1c beginning at age ten years. Annual serum TSH with reflex to thyroxine beginning at age ten years.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies annual metabolic and thyroid surveillance from age ten.

treatments/5.description: Beginning in childhood, annual fasting glucose, hemoglobin A1c, and thyroid testing support early detection and standard treatment of diabetes and hypothyroidism.

evidence.snippet: Cough assist devices, vibration vests, and daily nasal lavage for mucociliary clearance for bronchiectasis.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists the airway-clearance measures used for bronchiectasis.

treatments/6.description: Recurrent or chronic pulmonary disease is assessed at each visit. Bronchiectasis care can include cough-assist devices, vibration vests, and daily nasal lavage for mucociliary clearance.

evidence.snippet: There is limited literature about HSCT and BS for children
evidence.explanation: Establishes that transplantation is used in this population while the evidence base for it is acknowledged as thin.

evidence.snippet: In our experience, one patient underwent HSCT with a myeloablative conditioning regimen but died shortly after transplantation due to treatment-related toxicity, despite being in remission at the time.
evidence.explanation: A myeloablative transplant in remission ended in treatment-related death, which cuts against transplantation with full-intensity conditioning as a safe option here. One patient, so it bounds enthusiasm rather than establishing a rule.

treatments/7.description: Allogeneic transplantation is used for hematologic malignancy in Bloom syndrome, but the reported experience is small and toxicity is substantial, because conditioning regimens deliver exactly the DNA-damaging exposure these patients tolerate poorly. It is a specialist-directed option under active uncertainty rather than a standard-of-care recommendation.

evidence.snippet: A multidisciplinary team of oncologists and endocrinologists is best suited to care for this patient population.
evidence.explanation: States the co-management recommendation this treatment records.

evidence.snippet: Both patients experienced severe toxicities and exacerbation of endocrine comorbidities during chemotherapy.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the observation that motivates co-management, namely that pre-existing endocrine disease worsened under treatment in both reported patients.

treatments/8.description: The endocrinopathies that are already characteristic of Bloom syndrome, principally insulin-resistant diabetes, dyslipidemia, and hypothyroidism, are destabilized by cancer treatment, and steroid and asparaginase exposure add adrenal insufficiency and severe hypertriglyceridemia. Joint oncology and endocrinology management is recommended for the duration of therapy.

treatments/9.description: Bloom syndrome is autosomal recessive, so each subsequent sibling has a one-in-four recurrence risk. Once both familial BLM variants are known, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are available, and carrier screening panels commonly include the condition. Evaluating at-risk siblings also allows sun avoidance and cancer surveillance to start early.

evidence.snippet: we identified eight different heterozygous missense CDK8 substitutions, including 10 shown to have arisen de novo, in 12 unrelated subjects
evidence.explanation: Physical variant class in affected individuals.

steps/1.description: Heterozygous coding single-nucleotide substitutions alter conserved residues in or near the ATP-binding pocket. Their physical sequence changes are distinct from the resulting catalytic and developmental effects.

evidence.snippet: the substrate-binding site of the WT CDK8 protein can adopt more open conformations than its mutated counterparts
evidence.explanation: Structural-dynamics prediction.

steps/2.description: Molecular-dynamics models of Ser62Leu and Arg178Gln predict a less open substrate-binding region. Gross protein misfolding and loss of ATP binding were not observed in biochemical studies; restricted substrate access remains a mechanistic interpretation.

evidence.snippet: We observed that the cellular levels of pSTAT1 were reduced to a statistically significant extent, compared to WT, in all mutant-transfected cells
evidence.explanation: Variant activity in a double-knockout cell background.

evidence.snippet: Both the CDK8-G28A and CDK8-N156S mutations resulted in lower kinase activities compared with CDK8-WT
evidence.explanation: Autophosphorylation assay of later variants.

steps/3.description: Tested alleles reduce kinase output. Most founding variants approach the kinase-dead control in the STAT1 assay, whereas Phe97Leu and Ile223Met retain intermediate activity. Gly28Ala and Asn156Ser also reduce autophosphorylation. Protein stability and cyclin-C binding are retained, so this is not equivalent to complete loss of the gene product.

evidence.snippet: We observed that the cellular levels of pSTAT1 were reduced to a statistically significant extent, compared to WT, in all mutant-transfected cells
evidence.explanation: Direct substrate readout.

steps/4.description: Variant CDK8 produces less STAT1 Ser727 phosphorylation in SW620 cells lacking both endogenous CDK8 and CDK19. This is a measured biochemical readout, not evidence that STAT1 deficiency or immune dysfunction is the clinical disease mechanism.

evidence.snippet: we predict that up to 50% of CDK8 modules could be present in a kinase-inactive, non-productive state
evidence.explanation: Authors explicitly frame this as a prediction.

evidence.snippet: the observed reduction in phosphorylation in mixed samples did not obviously deviate from a linear response
evidence.explanation: The mixing assay did not establish a dominant-negative interaction.

steps/5.description: Retained cyclin-C/module association despite impaired catalysis could reduce availability of productive kinase modules. This proposed dominant-negative route remains unconfirmed: mixing reference and Ser62Leu constructs did not show a clearly nonlinear reduction in STAT1 phosphorylation.

evidence.snippet: Thus, a disruption of the proper activity of CDK8 could modify any of these developmental signaling networks.
evidence.explanation: Proposed developmental-signaling interpretation.

steps/6.description: CDK8 regulates transcription through Mediator and phosphorylation of multiple regulators. The relevant altered expression programs in patient neural and cardiac cells have not been identified. Candidate developmental pathways should not be treated as measured patient defects.

evidence.snippet: the inhibition of Cdk8 kinase activity by Senexin A induced structural anomalies in the heart and craniofacial cartilage of the zebrafish

evidence.snippet: We provide the first report to our knowledge of homozygous nonsense mutations in CHRNA1 and CHRND and show that they were lethal, whereas novel recessive missense mutations in RAPSN caused a severe but not necessarily lethal phenotype.
evidence.explanation: This study establishes that homozygous null CHRNA1 variants cause a lethal prenatal phenotype, consistent with severe loss of fetal AChR function.

steps/1.description: Biallelic null or functionally severe CHRNA1 variants disrupt the alpha-1 subunit of the fetal muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, preventing normal postsynaptic receptor function at the neuromuscular junction. This produces profound impairment of fetal neuromuscular transmission and places CHRNA1-related disease on a spectrum with later-onset congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by milder alleles.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that complete or severe functional disruption of fetal AChR causes lethal multiple pterygium syndrome whereas milder alterations result in fetal hypokinesia with inborn contractures or a myasthenic syndrome later in life.
evidence.explanation: This directly links severe fetal AChR dysfunction to the prenatal-lethal lethal multiple pterygium / fetal hypokinesia presentation and contrasts it with milder postnatal myasthenic phenotypes.

steps/2.description: Profound reduction of fetal neuromuscular transmission leads to markedly decreased fetal movement. Secondary consequences include multiple joint contractures, pterygia, edema or hydrops, craniofacial anomalies such as micrognathia, and pulmonary hypoplasia, yielding a prenatal-lethal multiple-pterygium / fetal akinesia deformation sequence presentation.

steps/1.description: Biallelic COX11 variants impair the copper metallochaperone that delivers copper to the CuB centre of the core catalytic subunit COX1, preventing assembly of a functional Complex IV holoenzyme. evidence.explanation: A third patient with Leigh-like features expands the encephalopathic phenotype of COX11-related disease.

steps/3.description: Infantile-onset mitochondrial encephalopathy is the defining clinical presentation of COX11-related disease; a later-reported patient showed Leigh-like features.

edges/1.description: Failure to metallate the CuB centre of COX1 yields a catalytically deficient Complex IV.

edges/2.description: Bioenergetic failure in the developing brain produces an infantile-onset mitochondrial encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic pathogenic variants in the COX11 protein were previously identified in two unrelated children with infantile-onset mitochondrial encephalopathies
evidence.explanation: Independent report confirming biallelic COX11 variants as the cause of the disorder.

evidence.snippet: the functional deficits observed in patient fibroblasts are recapitulated in yeast models
evidence.explanation: Yeast modelling of the patient variants supports their pathogenicity at the COX11 locus.

treatments/0.description: No curative therapy exists; management is supportive, addressing the encephalopathy and associated neurological features, with physiotherapy and rehabilitation and treatment of any metabolic decompensation.

evidence.snippet: mutant COX11 fibroblasts had decreased ATP levels which could be rescued by CoQ10
evidence.explanation: Provides the in vitro rationale for CoQ10 as a candidate metabolic therapy in COX11-related disease.

evidence.snippet: These results not only suggest that COX11 variants cause defects in energy production but reveal a potential metabolic therapeutic strategy for patients with COX11 variants
evidence.explanation: The authors frame CoQ10 rescue as a potential metabolic therapeutic strategy.

treatments/1.description: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) supplementation is a candidate metabolic strategy: in COX11-mutant patient fibroblasts the respiration-derived ATP deficit was rescued by CoQ10, despite COX11 having no known role in CoQ10 biosynthesis. This remains an experimental/investigational rationale rather than an established therapy.

evidence.snippet: The absence of COX16 protein expression leads to a complete loss of the holo-complex IV, as detected by Western blot in patient fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: Loss of COX16 abolishes the assembled holo-enzyme in patient fibroblasts, i.e. failed Complex IV biogenesis.

evidence.snippet: Lentiviral transduction of patient fibroblasts with wild-type COX16 complementary DNA rescued complex IV biosynthesis
evidence.explanation: Re-expression of wild-type COX16 restores Complex IV biosynthesis, confirming COX16 loss as the direct molecular lesion.

evidence.snippet: We hypothesize that COX16 could play a role in the copper delivery route of the COX2 module as part of the complex IV assembly
evidence.explanation: Localizes the COX16 lesion to the copper-delivery route of the COX2 assembly module.

evidence.snippet: COX16, a protein required for cytochrome c oxidase assembly, interacts specifically with newly synthesized COX2 and its copper center-forming metallochaperones SCO1, SCO2, and COA6
evidence.explanation: Defines the molecular role of COX16 in COX2 metallation/assembly that is lost in disease.

evidence.snippet: These findings implicate COX16 in CuA-site formation
evidence.explanation: COX16 is implicated in forming the copper CuA center of COX2, the step impaired by COX16 loss.

evidence.snippet: its ablation in HEK293 cells impairs COX assembly
evidence.explanation: Genetic ablation of COX16 in human cells impairs Complex IV assembly, supporting the assembly-factor role.

evidence.snippet: Its knockdown in C. elegans produces COX deficiency
evidence.explanation: COX16 knockdown in an animal model recapitulates COX deficiency, supporting conserved essentiality.

evidence.snippet: copper supplementation increases COX activity and restores normal steady state levels of COX subunits in COX16 knockout cells, indicating that, even in the absence of a canonical copper binding motif, COX16 could be involved in copper delivery to COX2
evidence.explanation: Copper rescue of COX16-null cells supports COX16's function in copper delivery to COX2.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss-of-function of COX16 removes a Complex IV assembly factor that interacts with newly synthesized COX2 and its copper-center-forming metallochaperones (SCO1, SCO2, COA6) and participates in copper delivery to COX2 / CuA-site formation. Loss of COX16 blocks formation of the COX2 subassembly module and produces complete loss of the holo-complex IV, i.e. failed Complex IV biogenesis with isolated Complex IV deficiency.

evidence.snippet: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, encephalopathy and severe fatal lactic acidosis, and isolated complex IV deficiency
evidence.explanation: Reduced Complex IV in these patients is the biochemical basis for impaired terminal electron transfer and the high-energy-tissue (cardiac, neural) phenotypes.

steps/2.description: Deficient Complex IV blocks electron transfer from cytochrome c to oxygen and the coupled proton pumping, collapsing oxidative ATP synthesis. High-energy tissues — heart and brain — are preferentially injured, producing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: severe fatal lactic acidosis
evidence.explanation: Severe fatal lactic acidosis is a defining metabolic feature of the index patients.

steps/3.description: The block in oxidative phosphorylation shifts pyruvate toward lactate, producing severe, fatal neonatal lactic acidosis with systemic metabolic decompensation and secondary liver dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: two unrelated patients with the homozygous nonsense variant c.244C>T(p. Arg82*) in COX16 with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, encephalopathy and severe fatal lactic acidosis, and isolated complex IV deficiency
evidence.explanation: The two index patients carrying the homozygous COX16 variant presented with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

steps/4.description: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy reported in the index COX16 patients.

evidence.snippet: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, encephalopathy and severe fatal lactic acidosis
evidence.explanation: Encephalopathy is reported as a presenting feature of the index patients.

steps/5.description: Encephalopathy as part of the COX16-related mitochondrial presentation.

evidence.snippet: severe fatal lactic acidosis
evidence.explanation: Severe fatal lactic acidosis is a presenting feature of the index patients.

steps/6.description: Severe, fatal neonatal lactic acidosis.

evidence.snippet: encephalopathy, cardiomyopathy, and liver dysfunction
evidence.explanation: Liver dysfunction is reported among the features of COX16 deficiency.

steps/7.description: Liver dysfunction accompanying the severe neonatal metabolic crisis.

evidence.snippet: isolated complex IV deficiency. The absence of COX16 protein expression leads to a complete loss of the holo-complex IV
evidence.explanation: Failed COX16-dependent assembly produces complete loss of the holo-complex IV and an isolated Complex IV deficiency, the basis for impaired terminal electron transfer.

edges/1.description: An unassembled, COX16-deficient Complex IV cannot transfer electrons to oxygen, impairing oxidative ATP synthesis.

edges/2.description: Impaired oxidative ATP synthesis forces anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactic acidosis.

edges/3.description: Chronic bioenergetic failure in cardiomyocytes drives hypertrophic remodeling.

edges/4.description: Energy deficit in high-demand neural tissue produces encephalopathy.

edges/5.description: Accumulated lactate produces the measured lactic acidosis.

edges/6.description: Energy failure and metabolic decompensation impair hepatocyte function, producing liver dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: the homozygous nonsense variant c.244C>T(p. Arg82*) in COX16
evidence.explanation: Defines the causal COX16 nonsense variant.

treatments/0.description: No curative therapy exists; management is supportive, directed at the metabolic decompensation and lactic acidosis, cardiac and neurologic surveillance, and multidisciplinary care. The reported neonatal presentation was fatal.

evidence.snippet: Genomic rearrangements lead to recurrent structural breakpoints within TERT promoter region, which correlates with highly elevated TERT expression and manifestation of kataegis, representing a mechanism of TERT upregulation in cancer distinct from previously observed amplifications and point mutations.
evidence.explanation: TCGA whole-genome sequencing establishes the structural-rearrangement route to TERT upregulation in chRCC and explicitly contrasts it with the amplification and point-mutation mechanisms seen elsewhere.

steps/2.description: chRCC reactivates telomerase by a mechanism distinct from the point mutations and amplifications that dominate other cancers: recurrent genomic rearrangements place structural breakpoints within the TERT promoter region, juxtaposing it with strong enhancers. The result is markedly elevated TERT expression accompanied by localized hypermutation (kataegis) at the breakpoint. This is the enhancer-hijacking route to replicative immortality.

evidence.snippet: The result is consistent that ChRCC originates from the distal nephron compared with other kidney cancers with more proximal origins.
evidence.explanation: TCGA multi-platform characterization of 66 tumors establishes the distal nephron origin of chRCC in contrast to the proximal origin of other renal cancers.

evidence.snippet: ChRCCs are considered to originate from the intercalated cell of distal tubules with two main morphological variants, classic and eosinophilic.
evidence.explanation: Independent review confirming the intercalated-cell origin at the cell-type level of granularity curated on this node.

steps/3.description: chRCC arises from the intercalated cells of the distal nephron and collecting duct. This is the single fact from which most of the rest of chRCC biology follows: the intercalated cell is mitochondria-rich, which anticipates the tumor's oxidative metabolic phenotype, and it is also the presumed cell of origin of renal oncocytoma, which is why the two tumors overlap so heavily on morphology and immunophenotype. Clear cell and papillary RCC instead arise from the proximal tubule.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that a specific combination of multiple chromosomal losses characterizes chromophobe renal cell carcinomas and may help to differentiate them unequivocally from other types of kidney cancer.
evidence.explanation: The original comparative genomic hybridization study establishing the specific multi-chromosome loss signature as characteristic of chRCC.

evidence.snippet: we have confirmed the high specificity of monosomies of chromosomes 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 17 and 21 in 70-93% of the chRCCs
evidence.explanation: SNP-array analysis of 30 chRCCs quantifies the frequency of each characteristic monosomy, supporting the 70-93% figure curated here.

evidence.snippet: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (chRCC) typically shows ~7 chromosome losses (1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 17, and 21) and ~31 exonic somatic mutations, yet carries ~5%-10% metastatic incidence.
evidence.explanation: Directly quantifies the defining juxtaposition of extensive chromosome loss with a low exonic mutation burden that this node models.

steps/4.description: The genomic hallmark of chRCC is the combined loss of entire chromosomes 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 17 and 21, present in 70-93% of tumors and specific enough to be used diagnostically against renal oncocytoma. What makes this pattern mechanistically unusual is its company: chRCC carries roughly seven chromosome losses alongside only about thirty exonic somatic mutations, so the dominant oncogenic signal is copy-number rather than point mutation. Roughly 40% of tumors have no identified driver mutation in any known oncogene or tumor suppressor, which implicates the aneuploidy itself as a primary transforming event. The upstream cause of the loss pattern is not established.

evidence.snippet: TP53 and PTEN are the two most frequently mutated genes in ChRCCs.
evidence.explanation: Establishes TP53 as the leading recurrently mutated gene in chRCC.

evidence.snippet: TP53 mutations (58%), PTEN mutations (24%), and imbalanced chromosome duplication (ICD, duplication of ≥ 3 chromosomes) (25%) were enriched in M-chRCC.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies TP53 mutation frequency in metastatic chRCC and its enrichment relative to non-metastatic disease.

steps/5.description: TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in chRCC. Mutation is enriched in higher-grade and metastatic tumors, where it reaches 58%, against roughly a third of unselected cases. Loss of p53-mediated transcriptional control removes the DNA-damage and apoptotic checkpoint that would otherwise constrain a cell carrying this degree of aneuploidy.

evidence.snippet: TP53 and PTEN are the two most frequently mutated genes in ChRCCs.
evidence.explanation: Supports PTEN as a leading recurrently mutated gene in chRCC. Marked PARTIAL because the review states the mutation frequency but does not itself demonstrate the downstream mTORC1 hyperactivation modeled here.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrate that TP53 mutations (58%), PTEN mutations (24%), and imbalanced chromosome duplication (ICD, duplication of ≥ 3 chromosomes) (25%) were enriched in M-chRCC.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies PTEN mutation in metastatic chRCC. INDIRECT for the same reason: it establishes the lesion, not the pathway-activation readout.

steps/6.description: Several independent lesions converge on constitutive mTORC1 signaling in chRCC: somatic PTEN loss (the second most frequently mutated gene, and 24% in metastatic tumors), somatic mutation of MTOR, TSC1, TSC2 or NRAS, and - in the hereditary setting - germline FLCN loss. This convergence is what makes mTOR inhibition the mechanistically motivated systemic option in chRCC, in contrast to the VEGF-directed strategies that follow from VHL-HIF biology in clear cell RCC.

evidence.snippet: Combined mtDNA and gene expression analysis implicates changes in mitochondrial function as a component of the disease biology, while suggesting alternative roles for mtDNA mutations in cancers relying on oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence.explanation: TCGA analysis directly implicates altered mitochondrial function in chRCC biology and identifies the tumor as one relying on oxidative phosphorylation rather than glycolysis.

evidence.snippet: We found 6 somatic nucleotide changes in 5 out of the 8 chromophobe RCCs.
evidence.explanation: Whole-mitochondrial-genome sequencing establishes that somatic mtDNA mutations occur in the majority of chRCCs. Marked PARTIAL because the same study explicitly declines to attribute a causal role to them.

steps/7.description: chRCC cells accumulate mitochondria and show near-universal upregulation of Krebs cycle and electron transport chain genes relative to normal kidney, together with the highest expression of mitochondrially encoded genes among RCC subtypes. Somatic mitochondrial DNA mutations, including frameshifting changes in complex I subunit genes, are found in the majority of tumors. This is a genuinely distinct metabolic state, not a variant of the glycolytic Warburg shift that characterizes VHL-mutant clear cell RCC, and it is why this entry does not conform to the aerobic-glycolysis node of the deregulated_cellular_energetics module. Whether the mtDNA mutations are drivers or passengers of this phenotype remains unresolved.

evidence.snippet: The aggregate literature suggests that chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is biologically a tumor of low malignant potential with reported 5-year and 10-year survival rates of 78% to 100% and 80% to 90%, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the low-malignant-potential behavior and the survival range curated on this node.

steps/8.description: The convergent result is a solitary, well-circumscribed renal cortical tumor that is frequently large at diagnosis yet behaves as a tumor of low malignant potential, with 5-year survival reported between 78% and 100%. The dissociation between tumor size and metastatic risk distinguishes chRCC from clear cell RCC and underlies its favorable prognosis.

evidence.snippet: Sarcomatoid change was present in 12/145 (8%) tumors.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the frequency of sarcomatoid change in a 145-case clinicopathologic series.

evidence.snippet: chromosomal gains are known to be associated with sarcomatoid ChRCCs
evidence.explanation: Supports the distinct copy-number profile of sarcomatoid chRCC relative to the loss-dominated conventional tumor.

steps/9.description: A minority of chRCC undergoes sarcomatoid (spindle-cell) transformation. This is the principal adverse prognostic event in the disease and converts an otherwise indolent tumor into aggressive, systemic-therapy-requiring disease. Unlike the conventional tumor, sarcomatoid chRCC is associated with chromosomal gains rather than the characteristic loss pattern.

evidence.snippet: our study provides genomic insights into the metastatic progression of chRCC and identifies TP53 mutations, PTEN mutations, and ICD as high-risk features
evidence.explanation: Identifies the three genomic features that distinguish metastatic from non-metastatic chRCC, which is what this node models.

steps/10.description: Between 5% and 10% of chRCC ultimately metastasizes. Metastatic tumors are genomically distinguishable from non-metastatic ones by enrichment for TP53 mutation, PTEN mutation and imbalanced chromosome duplication - the duplication of three or more chromosomes on top of the baseline loss pattern - and the presence of these features in a primary tumor is associated with worse survival.

edges/2.description: The intercalated cell of origin acquires the characteristic pattern of whole-chromosome losses.

edges/3.description: The mitochondria-rich character of the cell of origin is retained and amplified in the tumor.

edges/4.description: Chromosome 17 loss removes one TP53 allele, contributing to the inactivation of the p53 axis.

edges/5.description: Chromosome 10 loss removes one PTEN allele, contributing to release of the brake on PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling.

edges/6.description: The aneuploid genome supports outgrowth of the transformed clone.

edges/7.description: p53-axis loss is enriched in the aggressive, dedifferentiated subset.

edges/8.description: Loss of checkpoint control permits proliferation of the transformed clone.

edges/9.description: Constitutive mTORC1 output drives anabolic growth and proliferation.

edges/10.description: Telomerase reactivation removes the replicative limit on the tumor clone.

edges/11.description: Oxidative metabolism sustains the bioenergetic demands of the tumor.

edges/12.description: A minority of tumors undergo high-grade dedifferentiation.

edges/13.description: Dedifferentiated tumors account for a disproportionate share of metastatic chRCC.

evidence.snippet: TP53 mutations (58%), PTEN mutations (24%), and imbalanced chromosome duplication (ICD, duplication of ≥ 3 chromosomes) (25%) were enriched in M-chRCC.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies somatic TP53 mutation frequency in metastatic chRCC.

genes/0.notes: The most frequently mutated gene in chRCC. Reported in roughly a third of unselected TCGA cases and 58% of metastatic tumors, where it is one of three genomic high-risk features.

evidence.snippet: TP53 and PTEN are the two most frequently mutated genes in ChRCCs.
evidence.explanation: Establishes PTEN as one of the two leading recurrently mutated genes.

genes/1.notes: The second most frequently mutated gene in chRCC, and the somatic counterpart of the germline PTEN loss that predisposes to renal cell carcinoma in Cowden syndrome. PTEN loss releases the brake on PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling and is one of three genomic high-risk features in metastatic disease.

evidence.snippet: We describe the landscape of somatic genomic alterations of 66 chromophobe renal cell carcinomas (ChRCCs) on the basis of multidimensional and comprehensive characterization, including mtDNA and whole-genome sequencing. ... Genomic rearrangements lead to recurrent structural breakpoints within TERT promoter region, which correlates with highly elevated TERT expression and manifestation of kataegis, representing a mechanism of TERT upregulation in cancer distinct from previously observed amplifications and point mutations.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the chromophobe RCC somatic-genomics cohort and the TERT promoter rearrangement, expression and kataegis findings, including the contrast with amplification and point-mutation mechanisms. The excerpt supports a mechanism of TERT upregulation; tumor-driver interpretation also depends on that biological context.

genes/2.notes: Upregulated in chRCC by structural rearrangement of the promoter region rather than by the promoter point mutations or amplifications seen in other tumor types. The breakpoints are accompanied by localized hypermutation (kataegis).

evidence.snippet: Gene test confirmed a heterozygous germline FLCN nonsense mutation (c.1429C > T, p.Arg477Ter).
evidence.explanation: Documents a germline FLCN loss-of-function variant in a patient whose resected tumors were bilateral hybrid oncocytic/chromophobe tumors and chromophobe carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: chromophobe histologic cell types (oncocytic hybrid tumor); clear cell carcinoma and oncocytoma are also common.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes the renal tumor histology spectrum of BHD syndrome, in which chromophobe and hybrid oncocytic tumors predominate.

genes/3.notes: Germline FLCN loss of function causes Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, in which chRCC and hybrid oncocytic/chromophobe tumors are the dominant renal histologies. FLCN is not typically somatically mutated in sporadic chRCC, so this is a distinct hereditary route into the same histology.

evidence.snippet: Treatment options for RCC confined to the kidney include surgical resection with partial or radical nephrectomy
evidence.explanation: Establishes partial or radical nephrectomy as first-line treatment for kidney-confined renal cell carcinoma.

treatments/0.description: Surgical resection is the primary and usually curative treatment for localized chRCC. Partial nephrectomy is preferred where technically feasible, and is strongly favored in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, where further tumors are expected over the patient's lifetime and renal function must be preserved across repeated operations.

evidence.snippet: one subtype (chromophobe) in which everolimus was associated with a longer median progression-free survival than that of sunitinib.
evidence.explanation: The chromophobe-specific result from the only randomized comparison in this setting. Marked PARTIAL because it is a subgroup finding within a trial whose overall result favored sunitinib, not a powered chRCC-specific comparison.

evidence.snippet: chromophobe renal cell carcinoma is often found to have activating mutations in the PI3K-mTOR pathway and preclinical sensitivity to rapamycin analogues
evidence.explanation: States the mechanistic rationale this treatment is curated on - that chRCC carries PI3K-mTOR pathway activation and shows preclinical sensitivity to rapamycin analogues.

evidence.snippet: partial response was more frequent in cases with mTOR pathway mutations than in those without mutations
evidence.explanation: Links mTOR pathway mutation status to rapalog response in renal cell carcinoma, supporting the biomarker rationale. PARTIAL because the cohort is renal cell carcinoma broadly rather than chRCC specifically.

treatments/1.description: Everolimus is used in advanced and metastatic chRCC on the rationale that the tumor's recurrent lesions converge on mTORC1. Supporting evidence is indirect: the randomized ASPEN trial in non-clear cell RCC favored sunitinib overall while reporting treatment-effect heterogeneity across histologic subtypes, and no adequately powered randomized trial has tested mTOR inhibition in chRCC specifically.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Everolimus inhibits mTORC1, the node on which chRCC's recurrent PTEN, MTOR, TSC1, TSC2 and NRAS lesions converge. This is the mechanism-matched systemic option in chRCC, in contrast to the VEGF-directed therapy motivated by VHL-HIF biology in clear cell RCC.

evidence.snippet: In patients with metastatic non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma, sunitinib improved progression-free survival compared with everolimus.
evidence.explanation: The randomized trial's primary conclusion supports sunitinib in metastatic non-clear cell RCC, the population that includes chRCC.

treatments/2.description: VEGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib and cabozantinib are used in advanced chRCC largely by extrapolation from non-clear cell RCC guidelines. The mechanistic rationale is weaker here than in clear cell RCC: chRCC lacks the VHL-HIF-VEGF axis that makes clear cell tumors hypervascular, and responses are correspondingly less predictable.

open_questions/0.rationale: The chromosome-loss signature is the defining and near-pathognomonic feature of chRCC, yet no genome-maintenance defect, replication-stress lesion or checkpoint failure has been identified as its cause. This is why the entry does not declare conformance to the genome_instability_mutation module: that module's central node models chromosomal instability arising from defective repair and failed surveillance with an accompanying elevated mutation rate, and chRCC has the aneuploidy without the mutator phenotype - roughly seven chromosome losses against roughly thirty-one exonic somatic mutations. The question is mechanistically important because extensive chromosome loss normally imposes proteotoxic stress and impairs proliferation, so whatever permits chRCC to tolerate it is likely to be a genuine feature of the disease rather than an incidental one.

evidence.snippet: It was thought for many years that ChRCC exhibits a hypodiploid genome. Recent studies using advanced molecular genetics techniques have shown more complex and heterogenous pattern with frequent chromosomal gains.
evidence.explanation: Directly states the revision of the hypodiploid model that this discussion records as unsettled.

open_questions/1.rationale: The long-standing description of chRCC as a hypodiploid tumor comes from comparative genomic hybridization studies of the 1990s. Higher-resolution methods have since shown a more complex and heterogeneous picture in which chromosomal gains are also frequent, and gains are specifically associated with sarcomatoid tumors and with metastatic progression through imbalanced chromosome duplication. Whether hypodiploidy remains the right summary of chRCC genomics, or is better treated as the baseline state on which later gains are superimposed during progression, is unsettled and matters for how the diagnostic copy-number test is interpreted in aggressive tumors.

evidence.snippet: Although somatic mtDNA mutations are found in chromophobe RCCs, their role in the maintenance of tumor cell phenotype or in tumorigenesis remains to be elucidated.
evidence.explanation: The source study states the open question directly, which is what this discussion records.

open_questions/2.rationale: Somatic mtDNA mutations, including frameshifting changes in complex I subunit genes, are present in the majority of chRCCs, and the tumor shows the highest mitochondrial gene expression among RCC subtypes. But the intercalated cell of origin is itself mitochondria-rich, so an oxidative phenotype is the expected inheritance rather than necessarily an acquired one. The original sequencing study explicitly declined to assign a causal role. Resolving this matters therapeutically, because targeting mitochondrial metabolism has been proposed as a chRCC-specific vulnerability and that proposal presumes a driver role.

evidence.snippet: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), resulting from mutations in CYP11B1, a gene encoding 11β-hydroxylase, represents a rare autosomal recessive Mendelian disorder of aberrant sex steroid production.
evidence.explanation: Supports CYP11B1 loss as a steroidogenic enzyme-deficiency mechanism in the 11B-OHD subtype.

evidence.snippet: Clinically, affected female newborns are profoundly virilized (Prader score of 4/5), and both genders display significantly advanced bone ages and are oftentimes hypertensive.
evidence.explanation: Links the 11 beta-hydroxylase deficiency mechanism to virilization and hypertension in the human cohort.

steps/6.description: CYP11B1 pathogenic variants reduce steroid 11 beta-hydroxylase function, producing a rare CAH subtype with aberrant sex-steroid production, virilization, and mineralocorticoid precursor-mediated hypertension.

evidence.snippet: 3β-HSD deficiency, with an incidence of less than 1/1,000,000 live births, is characterized by impairment of both adrenal and gonadal steroid biosynthesis very early in life
evidence.explanation: Supports the combined adrenal and gonadal scope that distinguishes this node from the later single-branch enzymatic blocks.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in HSD3B2 cause a rare form of CAH.
evidence.explanation: Establishes HSD3B2 as the gene whose loss produces this node.

evidence.snippet: In this enzyme deficiency, the production of cortisol, aldosterone, progesterone, androgens and estrogens is affected
evidence.explanation: Substantiates this node's claim that the blocked step is shared by the glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid and sex-steroid branches.

steps/7.description: HSD3B2 pathogenic variants reduce the adrenal and gonadal 3-beta-hydroxy-delta5-steroid dehydrogenase that converts delta-5 precursors to their delta-4 counterparts. The step is shared by the glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid and sex-steroid branches, so unlike the 21- and 11-beta-hydroxylase blocks this one impairs gonadal as well as adrenal steroidogenesis. The placental isozyme HSD3B1 is a different gene and is not implicated.

evidence.snippet: Patients with LCAH, which develops due to steroidogenic acute regulatory protein deficiency, typically present with salt wasting in the first year of life. It is characterized by complete or near-complete deficiency of adrenal and gonadal steroid hormones and progressive accumulation of cholesterol esters in the adrenal gland.
evidence.explanation: Supports both consequences this node asserts: near-complete steroid-output failure and cholesterol ester accumulation in the adrenal gland.

evidence.snippet: The classical form usually occurs with loss-of-function in the StAR gene
evidence.explanation: Establishes STAR loss of function as the lesion behind this node.

evidence.snippet: StAR-mediated transport of cholesterol to the inner mitochondrial membrane is essential for steroidogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Substantiates the cholesterol-delivery step this node's description places above every enzymatic block in the entry.

steps/8.description: Loss of the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein removes the delivery of cholesterol to the inner mitochondrial membrane, where side-chain cleavage begins. This node sits above every enzymatic block in this entry: the substrate never reaches the first committed step, so adrenal and gonadal steroid output fails near-completely and unesterified cholesterol accumulates as esters in the adrenal cortex, giving the lipoid form its name.

evidence.snippet: all cytochrome P450 enzymes located in the endoplasmic reticulum get electrons for their catalytic activities from the co-factor
evidence.explanation: States the shared-electron-donor role that makes a single POR lesion reach several steroidogenic steps.

evidence.snippet: The main microsomal POR-dependent enzymes are involved in the biosynthesis of steroid hormones in both the adrenal cortex and gonads (CYP17A1, CYP19A1, CYP21A2, and CYP15A1)
evidence.explanation: Names CYP17A1 and CYP21A2 as POR-dependent, which is the evidence for the two downstream edges drawn from this node.

steps/9.description: POR pathogenic variants reduce the NADPH-dependent electron donor that every endoplasmic-reticulum cytochrome P450 requires for catalysis. This is the only lesion in this entry that reaches more than one enzymatic node: the same defect partially disables CYP17A1 and CYP21A2 together, which is why POR deficiency presents as a combined rather than a single-step block, and why it also affects aromatase and hepatic drug-metabolising P450s that lie outside adrenal steroidogenesis altogether.

evidence.snippet: 17α-Hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency (17OHD) caused by mutations in the CYP17A1 gene is a rare form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia typically characterised by cortisol deficiency, mineralocorticoid excess and sex steroid deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Supports CYP17A1 loss as a rare CAH mechanism with the expected cortisol, mineralocorticoid, and sex-steroid pattern.

steps/10.description: CYP17A1 pathogenic variants reduce steroid 17 alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase activity, causing a rare CAH subtype characterized by cortisol deficiency, sex-steroid deficiency, and mineralocorticoid excess. As with the CYP21A2 node, this is the enzymatic block rather than the gene lesion, and POR deficiency reaches it by removing the enzyme's electron supply rather than by altering CYP17A1 itself.

evidence.snippet: 21OHD is due to an insufficiency of 21-hydroxylase enzyme, which is encoded by the CYP21A2 gene and involved in cortisol and aldosterone production.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that CYP21A2-encoded 21-hydroxylase is required for cortisol and aldosterone production.

steps/11.description: Loss of CYP21A2 21-hydroxylase activity impairs adrenal steroidogenesis, reducing cortisol and, in severe classic disease, aldosterone production. The node is the enzymatic block, not the gene lesion, and it has two inbound routes: a biallelic CYP21A2 variant, which is the usual one and the reason the node is named after the gene, and loss of electron supply from POR, which reduces the same enzyme's catalysis without any CYP21A2 variant. The node name is kept because `kb/node_classes/pathograph_node_classes.txt` cites it as a worked example.

evidence.snippet: CAH is characterized by the overproduction of androgen, along with variable degrees of cortisol and aldosterone deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Summarizes the core hormonal abnormalities linking cortisol and aldosterone deficiency with androgen excess.

steps/12.description: Deficient cortisol removes negative feedback on ACTH secretion; aldosterone deficiency in salt-wasting disease causes electrolyte and volume instability.

evidence.snippet: Cortisol deficiency removes normal feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis leading to elevations in ACTH and adrenal androgen levels
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the human mechanism: loss of cortisol feedback drives ACTH elevation, adrenal hyperplasia, and androgen excess.

evidence.snippet: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) is an autosomal recessive disorder impairing cortisol synthesis due to reduced enzymatic activity. This leads to persistent adrenocortical overstimulation and the accumulation of precursors before the blocked enzymatic step.
evidence.explanation: The humanized mouse-model abstract summarizes how reduced enzyme activity drives persistent adrenal stimulation and precursor accumulation.

steps/13.description: Persistent adrenal stimulation and blocked steroidogenic flux promote adrenal cortical hyperplasia and excess androgen production.

evidence.snippet: Non-classic CAH, a milder form of CAH, is usually manifested later in life and is a common differential diagnosis of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome and should be actively evaluated during initial studies of clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism.
evidence.explanation: Supports late-presenting hyperandrogenism in nonclassic CAH and its clinical overlap with PCOS.

steps/14.description: Excess adrenal androgen exposure causes prenatal genital virilization and later hyperandrogenic features such as hirsutism, acne, menstrual irregularity, and infertility.

evidence.snippet: The age at diagnosis can provide some information about underlying mutations, with those diagnosed at birth/early infancy more likely to have severe enzymatic defects, which may include adrenal insufficiency, sexual development disorders, short stature in adulthood, hirsutism, and a higher risk for metabolic syndrome and infertility.
evidence.explanation: Identifies adrenal insufficiency among severe early-diagnosed CAH manifestations.

evidence.snippet: 17α-Hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency (17OHD) caused by mutations in the CYP17A1 gene is a rare form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia typically characterised by cortisol deficiency, mineralocorticoid excess and sex steroid deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Supports cortisol deficiency, the adrenal-insufficiency component, in CYP17A1-related CAH.

steps/15.description: Cortisol deficiency is a core feature of classic CAH and can present in neonates or early infancy in severe forms; rare enzyme defects such as CYP17A1 deficiency can also produce cortisol deficiency.

evidence.snippet: 21OHD is due to an insufficiency of 21-hydroxylase enzyme, which is encoded by the CYP21A2 gene and involved in cortisol and aldosterone production.

evidence.snippet: Over 95% of deleterious variants leading to 21OHD are attributable to intergenic recombination events where microconversions, consisting in the transfer to CYP21A2 of deleterious variants usually present in the CYP21A1P pseudogene, represent 70% to 75%
evidence.explanation: The quantitative basis for this record's claim that the CYP21A2 lesion is predominantly gene conversion from the CYP21A1P pseudogene rather than independent mutation.

evidence.snippet: A consequence of this phenomenon is that a small group of pathogenic variants with recognized phenotypic effects is detected in all populations
evidence.explanation: Supports the first practical consequence recorded in this record's notes.

evidence.snippet: Only 5% to 10% of small pathogenic variants affecting the CYP21A2 gene are not the result of genetic conversions
evidence.explanation: Substantiates the residual fraction of CYP21A2 alleles that arise outside the gene-conversion and crossing-over mechanisms.

evidence.snippet: A nonuniform meiotic crossing-over event is responsible for 20% to 25% of the remaining intergenic recombinations.
evidence.explanation: Substantiates the crossing-over share, and with the microconversion figure above accounts for the recombination total this record states.

evidence.snippet: a 30-kb deletion within RCCX region, encompassing the 3′ end of CYP21A1P, all the C4B gene, and the 5′ end of the CYP21A2 gene, leaves the TNXB gene intact
evidence.explanation: Substantiates the chimeric-gene and 30-kb deletion product of the crossing-over mechanism.

evidence.snippet: next-generation sequencing (NGS) is not yet recommended for CYP21A2 genotyping
evidence.explanation: Supports the second practical consequence: the gene-pseudogene homology makes routine short-read sequencing unsafe for this locus.

evidence.snippet: NGS, in the current state of the art, can identify pathogenic variants of the pseudogene and contribute to an inadequate molecular diagnosis
evidence.explanation: States the specific failure mode - pseudogene variants miscalled as gene variants.

evidence.snippet: MLPA is recommended as the first step in 21OHD molecular diagnosis to determine the exact copy number of genes and pseudogenes within the RCCX region
evidence.explanation: Substantiates the recommended genotyping approach named in this record's notes.

genes/0.notes:
The lesion type here is unlike the rest of this entry's genes. CYP21A2 sits in the RCCX copy-number-variable module of the MHC class III region beside an inactive, highly homologous pseudogene, CYP21A1P. Most disease alleles are therefore not independent new mutations but transfers of the pseudogene's own deleterious variants into the functional gene: the cited review attributes over 95% of deleterious 21OHD alleles to intergenic recombination, of which microconversions from the pseudogene are 70% to 75% and non-uniform meiotic crossing-over - which produces CYP21A1P/CYP21A2 chimeric genes and a 30-kb deletion - is 20% to 25%. Only 5% to 10% of small pathogenic variants arise outside these recombination events.
Two practical consequences follow and are the reason this is recorded rather than left implicit. First, a small recurrent set of pathogenic variants is seen in every population, because they are the pseudogene's variants rather than population-specific founder alleles. Second, the homology defeats ordinary sequencing: the review states that next-generation sequencing is not yet recommended for CYP21A2 genotyping because it can call pseudogene variants as gene variants, and that MLPA plus selective long-range amplification is the recommended approach.

Because the enzyme acts at the delta-5 to delta-4 conversion shared by all three steroid classes, the block is earlier in the pathway than the 21- and 11-beta-hydroxylase blocks and impairs gonadal as well as adrenal steroidogenesis.

evidence.snippet: Patients with LCAH, which develops due to steroidogenic acute regulatory protein deficiency, typically present with salt wasting in the first year of life. It is characterized by complete or near-complete deficiency of adrenal and gonadal steroid hormones and progressive accumulation of cholesterol esters in the adrenal gland.
evidence.explanation: Supports both the near-complete steroid-output failure and the cholesterol ester accumulation this record attributes to loss of cholesterol delivery.

evidence.snippet: Hovever in most patients with LCAH, the defect is found in StAR not the CYP11A1 gene for P450scc

genes/4.notes: STAR is the one gene in this entry that encodes neither an enzyme nor an enzyme's electron donor: the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein delivers cholesterol to the inner mitochondrial membrane, so its loss starves the first committed step rather than blocking a later one. That places the defect above every enzymatic block modelled here and explains the near-complete loss of adrenal and gonadal steroid output and the cholesterol ester accumulation that gives the lipoid form its name. A minority of clinically lipoid CAH is due to CYP11A1 rather than STAR; MONDO has no congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia child term for the CYP11A1 form (its only CYP11A1 CAH classes are non-human-animal ones), so no subtype row is recorded for it here.

Within this entry that makes POR the only gene whose lesion reaches more than one enzymatic node, which is how it is wired in the pathograph.
